title: Data cleaning and string operations
text:
When two datasets have been processed separately, how can we tell whether their columns still mean the same thing?
We will turn messy talk metadata into repeatable cleaning rules. String operations provide the hands-on example. We will then compare two versions of a pipeline and decide which results are compatible.

title: Data cleaning and string operations
section: Warmup: missingness in the last lecture
text:
Warmup: missingness in the last lecture
We have word_count (\(Y\)), recorded duration (\(X\)), and an indicator \(R=1\) if word_count is missing.
An import bug makes word_count more likely to be missing for talks with long recorded durations. The bug does not use the word count itself.
With a partner: Is this MCAR, MAR, or MNAR under the stated mechanism? What would a plot of missingness by duration help you check? What could it not establish?


Think 45 seconds. Compare 45 seconds. Share one reason.

title: Data cleaning and string operations
section: Warmup: one defensible answer
text:
Warmup: one defensible answer
Under the stated mechanism, \(P(R=1\mid Y,X)\) varies with observed duration \(X\), but not with \(Y\) after accounting for \(X\). That is MAR, not MCAR.
A plot can show whether missingness varies with recorded duration. It cannot prove that missingness does not also depend on the unobserved word counts.
Today’s records include a missing speaker. Cleaning should preserve that uncertainty, rather than invent a name.

A numeric rule also needs a reference

\[z = \frac{x - 2000}{1000}\]

title: Data cleaning and string operations
section: Follow along: put the rules in a function
text:
Follow along: put the rules in a function
def clean_talks(raw):
    result = raw.copy()
    result["speaker_key"] = (
        result["speaker"].astype("string").str.strip().str.lower()
    )
    result["word_count"] = pd.to_numeric(result["word_count"])
    result["word_scaled"] = (result["word_count"] - 2000) / 1000
    return result

cleaned = clean_talks(reference)
Predict: Does reference gain a speaker_key column? Why?

The code can be identical while the numbers have different meanings. A usable record includes the pipeline version and the fitted values or reference identifier.


Our code explicitly freezes 1000 and 3000 from the reference batch; it does not fit a new scale to each incoming batch.

title: Data cleaning and string operations
section: Compatibility: a working answer
text:
Compatibility: a working answer







Column
Decision




talk_id, original speaker, word_count
Combine if they still represent the same fields and units; check IDs and counts.


speaker_key
Rerun the v2 rule on the old records, then check matching keys.


word_scaled
Rescale the old raw counts using the same saved v2 reference values.



Keep raw data so a changed rule can be rerun. With preserved input columns, we can also rerun only the affected steps. Without the original text, some changes may be impossible to reconstruct.

title: Data cleaning and string operations
section: What to record with a processed batch
text:
What to record with a processed batch
pipeline_version: talks-v2
scaling_reference: reference-T01-T03
mean/std from that reference: 2000 / 1000   (used in v1)
min/max from that reference: 1000 / 3000    (used in v2)
We also retain the raw table and the code that defines each version. Version labels summarize decisions; they do not replace the code or scaling values.

title: Data cleaning and string operations
section: Exit check
text:
Exit check
An old table has v1 speaker_key and word_scaled. A new table has v2 columns with those same names.

Which original fields would you preserve before combining the tables?
Which processed fields need new values, and which saved numeric values would you use?
If a new talk has 3500 words, is v2’s value of 1.25 an error?
